en: Sutta Nipāta 4.13 Mahābyūhasutta “Whosoever among these are clinging to views, [they are lost].”
They dispute, saying, "This alone is the truth";
they all bring upon themselves blame,
yet they also receive praise therein.
“Indeed, this is trifling and not enough for peace;
I declare that there are two fruits of dispute.
Seeing even this, one should not engage in dispute.”
Beholding the secure ground free from dispute:
"Whatever conventional designations there are among ordinary people,
the wise man does not adhere to any of them."
“He who is without means— what means could he employ,
not finding contentment in what is seen and heard?
“Those for whom virtue is supreme say that purity comes through restraint.”
Having taken up the wind, they are established;
right here we shall train for its purification,
led toward existence by those skilled in the noble declarations.
If one has passed away from a state of virtue,
one trembles, having failed in one's action;
one yearns and aspires for purity.
Having fallen away from the Teacher while living abroad from home,
one has abandoned all rules and observances,
as well as this karma— both blameworthy and blameless.
Not aspiring for purity or impurity,
one should live detached, seeking after peace; or,
depending upon that which is loathsome, one should practice.
Or else, regarding what is seen, heard, or sensed,
those who look upward toward higher realms praise purity;
they are not free from craving for various states of existence.
For one who harbors longings, there is indeed yearning and even trembling over what has been planned;
yet for him who has no passing away or rebirth here, there is none.
“By what could one pierce it,
or where could one lament? “Some call this Dhamma supreme,
while others call that very same thing inferior.”
"Which of these doctrines is true?
For all of them proclaim themselves to be virtuous.
Each indeed says its own teaching is complete."
But they say that the Dhamma of another is inferior;
thus, quarreling and disputing,
each proclaims their own convention as the truth.
If one who is inferior were not to excel through disparaging another,
no one would distinguish themselves in the teachings;
for many indeed preach the Dhamma to others.
Though they speak with great confidence regarding their own lowly status,
even their worship of the True Dhamma is exactly like the way they praise their own bodies.
All doctrines might indeed be true,
for their purity is each person's own private experience.
A brahmin has no need to rely on others.
Having discerned among phenomena what has been grasped,
he has therefore transcended disputes,
for he does not see any other phenomenon as superior.
"I know, I see it is exactly so;
yet some, through their views, declare that purity comes thereby.
But if he has truly seen anything, what indeed would that have to do with him?"
Having bypassed this, they claim purity through something else.
A person seeing will perceive name-and-form;
having seen it, he will know these very things.
Whether one sees much or little,
the wise do not say that purity comes thereby;
for one who speaks with dogmatic insistence is not easily led to what is wholesome.
Placing his preconceived views before him,
whatever he relies upon there, proclaiming it as beautiful,
he speaks of purity, having seen it thus.
The Brahmin does not enter into conceptual construction,
nor does he rely on views, nor is he a kinsman of mere knowledge;
having understood the various conventional designations, he...
I think he maintains equanimity toward grasping.
Having relinquished all bonds here in the world,
the sage does not side with any faction amidst the various kinds of disputes.
He who is equanimous toward the good and the bad,
not grasping but rather letting go— I consider him one who has abandoned former defilements and does not create new ones.
Neither driven by desire nor a speaker of dogmatic assertions,
that wise one, liberated from all views and free from self-reproach,
is not defiled by the world.
He has become free from enmity toward all phenomena—
whatever is seen, heard, or sensed.
That sage, having laid down his burden, is utterly liberated.
“Neither is he one who imagines, nor is he one who is inactive, nor is he one who yearns.
Thus ends the thirteenth discourse, the Mahābyūhasutta.
